analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to get your consent before scanning and storing your face data.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, without a single vote in the Senate.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban companies from collecting face-scan data unless they first tell you, in plain language, what the technology can and cannot do and get your explicit agreement. It would also bar companies from reusing your face data for purposes you were not told about, sharing it with other companies without a separate yes from you, or refusing you service unless you consent. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rules, and regulators would write follow-up standards for data security and retention.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose faces are scanned — shoppers, social media users, and anyone walking into a store or past a camera with face recognition. The bill gives them the right to say no before a company converts their face into a permanent identifier, and it stops the silent reuse and resale of that data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shoppers, social media users, camera subjects

how_it_helps.text: Companies could not knowingly collect facial recognition data without explicit, individual, voluntary agreement after providing plain-language notice of what the data will be used for [S3].
Companies could not reuse face data for a purpose different from the one disclosed, or share it with an unaffiliated third party without separate consent [S3].
Companies could not condition service on a user consenting to waive privacy rights, and could not cut off a customer who refuses [S3].

A human would have to review any final decision based on facial recognition output that could cause material physical or financial harm, and providers of the technology would have to open it to independent accuracy and bias testing [S3].
The Federal Trade Commission would enforce violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents [S3].
The bill explicitly preserves stronger state privacy laws rather than preempting them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect, store, or process facial recognition data — social media platforms, camera and software vendors, and retailers that scan shoppers' faces. They would bear the cost of consent systems, plain-language notices, data security standards, and possible FTC or state enforcement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies that scan and store faces

drawbacks.text: The bill excludes federal, state, and local governments, law enforcement, national security, and intelligence agencies entirely [S3], so it leaves untouched the most powerful and least accountable uses of facial recognition — police and government face databases.

It exempts 'security applications' — loss prevention and detection of shoplifting and fraud — from the consent requirement [S3], meaning stores could keep scanning faces to catch theft without asking anyone.

The bill relies on consent notices and gives the FTC enforcement power, but it does not create a private right of action, so individual people could not sue a company that scanned their face without permission; only the FTC or a state attorney general could act [S3].
An honest supporter would concede that consent-notice regimes in privacy law often become legal boilerplate that users click through without reading, limiting the practical protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people scanned by commercial facial recognition, the benefit is a real right to say no before their face becomes a permanent database entry. The most serious design gap is scope, not substance: by excluding every government agency and all security uses, the bill addresses the commercial side of face scanning while leaving the government side unregulated, so it is a meaningful but partial fix.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Introduced March 14, 2019 by Senator Roy Blunt (R-MO) together with Senator Brian Schatz (D-HI), and read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S1] [S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote is recorded in the bill's complete action history [S5].
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021, and the bill was not reintroduced on the record within that Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from scanning faces — social media platforms, facial recognition vendors, and retailers running face-based surveillance — came out ahead, because they kept operating under the same patchwork of state rules and no federal consent requirement for two more years.

industries.industry: Companies that deploy facial recognition on customers (social media platforms, retailers, venue operators)
industries.note: They would lose the ability to convert customers' faces into permanent identifiers without explicit consent, and to reuse or share that data. For ordinary people, that is exactly the protection the bill exists to create, so the industry's interest runs against the public's here.

The bill imposes compliance costs and mandatory openness to independent accuracy and bias testing, but it does not ban the technology; a vendor that built reliable consent tools could keep selling into a regulated market.

The bill expressly excludes all government agencies, so police and intelligence face-scanning programs continue untouched while commercial uses are constrained — the public gets protection from the smaller half of the threat.
Security applications aimed at shoplifting and fraud are exempted from the consent requirement, so stores can keep scanning faces without asking, and the bill locks that carve-out in from day one.
